questions.q: What does `sshd -t` do, and why run it before restarting the SSH service?
options: It disables password authentication temporarily for testing
It checks sshd_config for syntax errors without restarting the service, catching a mistake before it breaks future connections
It tests whether the current user has a valid SSH key
It immediately restarts sshd and applies all pending changes
questions.explain: sshd -t validates the configuration file's syntax without reloading the service, so a typo is caught before it can lock out every future connection.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of setting `PermitRootLogin no`?
options: It automatically changes the SSH port to a non-default value
It forces administrators to log in as a named user and sudo to root, leaving a record of which account performed privileged actions
It disables SSH entirely for the root account on all systems
It has no real effect since root can always log in regardless
questions.explain: Without direct root login, every privileged action requires a named-user login followed by sudo, which both removes a single point of total compromise and creates accountability.

questions.q: What does changing the default SSH port actually accomplish, and what does it NOT accomplish?
options: It reduces automated scanning noise hitting port 22, but it is not real security since a determined attacker can still scan for the open port
It automatically encrypts SSH traffic more strongly than the default port
It completely prevents any attacker from ever finding the SSH service
It disables the need for key-based authentication
questions.explain: Moving off port 22 cuts down on opportunistic bot/scanner noise in the logs, but a targeted attacker can still find an open SSH service on any port with a scan.

questions.q: How do AllowUsers and DenyUsers interact with key-based authentication?
options: They replace the need for SSH keys entirely
AllowUsers and DenyUsers can never be used on the same server at the same time
They are checked after standard authentication as a hard backstop — a user denied here is rejected even with a valid key
They only apply to password authentication, never to key-based login
questions.explain: AllowUsers is an explicit allow-list and DenyUsers an explicit deny-list; both act as a backstop checked after authentication, so a denied account is rejected regardless of having a valid key.

questions.q: What is the safe order of operations before setting PasswordAuthentication no and restarting sshd?
options: Confirm key-based login already works from a second, still-open session, run sshd -t, restart sshd, then verify a brand-new connection succeeds before closing the original session
Set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd immediately from the only open session
There is no risk to changing this setting, since SSH automatically falls back to password auth if keys fail
Disable the firewall first, then change the setting
questions.explain: Verifying key auth works from a second open session before restarting sshd, and confirming a fresh connection succeeds before closing anything, is what prevents accidentally locking yourself out of the server.
